I was talking to my mom. She just recently got a new position within the company she's been working for for years. She showed me the social media contract they make her sign. Thing was kind of creepy to be honest. I told her that I believed a company can't limit your speech during hours that you aren't on the clock or on their premises. She disagreed. What do you think?
Should companies be able to limit speech during non-work hours?

Places can fire you for any reason. If I go out in a McDonald's uniform and say all these horrible things about the company, can you really blame them for firing me? I don't agree with it, but they are well within their right to do so. A step above would be the military. If you say something off-duty that makes your branch, the military, or the US look bad they have every right to kick you out or even put you in military prison.

(disclaimer: I don't work at McDonalds.)

I have a huge problem with this. It does not take much for a certain group to attack someone on twitter because they disagree with something they said. News articles are written within hours and it leads to a lot of people's lives being screwed with as employers won't defend them because it looks bad for companies. Unless you are breaking the law by promoting hate speech, or targeting individuals with an intent to harm them in some way, companies should not be able to restrict or act on anything you say during non-work hours. It is a restriction of free speech.

Where would you draw the line? Can you bash your company on social media? What if you made a page to protest the company? Why would I keep you? You definitely aren't in the company's best interest. The best part is your mom didn't have to sign that contract if she didn't agree with it. She most likely wouldn't be given the position but the choice was still hers.

Even if you don't indent it you represent the company you work for. If you go and say something stupid while dressed in that uniform, talking to a client or whatever it could adversely effect the company and they don't want that. That's why the contracts are so invasive and why I can't blame a company for having such things. However I think it's dumb and as a culture we need to grow a thicker skin.

Yes and no. The question is - is it justified?

Like @G4 said, talking about a company and criticizing it while being an employee puts the company in an odd position. On one hand, you're a worker. On the other, you're bad press. If the company decides they don't want that, they should have the right to fire you.

On the other hand, they decide what's considered bad. So the company can one day decide that a certain political ideology is bad, and ban it. Should it stop you from talking about the subject? In my opinion no. Because it doesn't affect the company.

At the end of the day, the company that hires you only sees what you want them to see. There are privacy settings, there's a contract that you sign. If you don't agree with the terms, you can simply decide not to sign the contract. I've heard some companies allow you to negotiate the terms of your employment? So that's worth a shot as well.

If you have a public position, such as the CEO of MS, then yes they should limit your public speech.

For the average no-name joe or anonymous or private postings they can fuck off.
Out of curiosity's sake would you post the contract? Of course, redact important information.

The real problem is of course political correctness culture, that is why companies feel compelled to it.

To answer your question, after my political plug, no, they should not be allowed. No pay, no say.

It depends. If you have a Twitter bio that says "employee of COMPANY NAME", then you are publicly drawing attention to the company and shouldn't be surprised if they don't want to be associated with certain behavior.

Do you live in a right-to-work state? If you do, then yes, unfortunately they should have the right. It's the state law.

Anywhere else and I don't think a company should be able to fire an employee for anything done that wasn't....expressly in the hiring contract.

You, Lullabyt , asked a good question. It has roots in human rights where it opposes the rights of business. I personally agreed that there should be a rule of silence about all that goes on "at the company" social media and all. But when I really think about it I see how this would be a reduction of the personal "sphere of influence". We would be giving away our right to speak about a third of our life. Fuck it I say...Sorry boss but this is the new world.

It really depends on the position. If you are representing the company then they have a rather large stake in what you're saying, and will end up facing the same consequences for anything non-PC you say that you do, unless they denounce and fire you (and maybe even then). The contract just sounds like a way to ensure that they can distance themselves safely (without your mom suing them) if she screws up and gets an angry mob on her.
I believe you should not be punished for saying anything that is factually true and unbiased. Aside from that, I believe it is difficult to draw a clear line.
Companies worry about whistle blowers for one thing.
